Reconcile a cash flow statement, and tie it to the balance sheet

Source: R/check_cashflow.R
check_cashflow.Rd

A cash flow statement can be wrong in a way its own arithmetic never shows. Move an amount from one activity to another and every total still adds up: the three activities still sum to the change in cash, and the change still carries last year's cash to this year's. So this asks two kinds of question. Does the statement agree with itself? And does it agree with the balance sheet it was drawn up from?

Usage

check_cashflow(x, by = NULL, tol = 1, rel = 0.05)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl(), with the taxonomy on it.

by

Columns identifying one statement instance. NULL, the default, uses whichever of file and basis the table has.

tol

Absolute tolerance in the reporting currency. Default 1.

rel

Relative tolerance for "debt vs balance", as a share of the larger of the two figures. Debt moves for reasons that move no cash, and a krone's tolerance would flag every company with a lease. Default 0.05.

Value

A tibble with one row per check and statement instance: the by columns, the key, check, reported (the figure the cash flow statement gives), expected (what the rest of the filing says it should be), residual (reported - expected), adjustment, offset_by and verdict. A filing with no cash flow statement has no rows.

The case it was written for

In its 2025 group accounts, Greenland Airports – Mittarfeqarfiit A/S (CVR 12859724) reported "Optagelse af langfristet gaeld" of DKK 1,157 million under financing. The group's long-term liabilities, read off the balance sheet in the same filing, rose by 793 million. The other 364 million was not debt. It shows up again in investing, as "Indtaegtsfoert anlaegstilskud" -364 million, a grant taken to income, tagged in the XBRL as SaleOfOtherCompany. Taking a grant to income moves no cash at all, and a sale does not take cash out. Sermitsiaq reported the misclassification in September 2026, and the company said it would correct it in the next year's report.

Every internal check passes on that filing. The activities sum to the change in cash, the change rolls forward, and the closing cash equals the balance sheet's to the krone. The error shows up only when the cash flow is held against the balance sheet, and that comparison is what this function adds.

The checks

One row per check per filing, in check:

  • "activities" – operating, investing and financing sum to the change in cash, before the effect of exchange rates where the filing states it.

  • "rollforward" – the opening cash plus the change is the closing cash. Whether the change already includes the exchange rate adjustment is the filer's reading, so both are tried, and "agrees, adjusted" with adjustment = "exchange rates" says the adjustment was needed.

  • "cash vs balance" – the closing cash in the cash flow statement is the cash in the balance sheet. A filing may count securities as cash and an overdraft against it, so "agrees, adjusted" means one of those adjustments closes the gap and adjustment names it.

  • "untagged: investing", "untagged: financing" – how much of an activity's total no tagged line accounts for. On its own this is not an error: a filer may leave a line untagged, or tag it with an element the taxonomy places elsewhere. But a reclassification has to leave one somewhere, and this is where it lands.

  • "sign: investing", "sign: financing" – one row per line whose sign contradicts its element: a sale, a proceeds or a raising of debt that took cash out. elementid names the line. Mistagging is common and usually harmless, so this is a lead and not a verdict on the filing.

  • "debt vs balance" – net borrowing in the cash flow statement against the change in long-term liabilities, including their short-term part, in the balance sheet.

  • Six more ties to the rest of the filing, each comparing magnitudes: "depreciation vs income" (the add-back against the income statement's charge), "purchases vs note: tangible" and "... intangible" (cash spent against the fixed asset note's additions), "capital vs equity" (a cash capital increase against the change in contributed capital and share premium), "dividends vs proposed" (paid this year against proposed at the end of the last) and "inventories vs balance". The verdict is "agrees", "cash flow larger" or "cash flow smaller".

The ties differ from the internal checks in one respect. Each has a known reason to differ – an asset leased rather than bought, debt converted to equity, an extraordinary dividend – so they are judged within rel rather than to the krone, and the verdict says which way a gap runs, because the direction is what tells a reason from a mistake.

For debt, "owed more than borrowed" is the common case: the liability grew by more than the cash raised, and a lease explains it. "fell more than repaid" is a reclassification or a conversion. "borrowed more than owed" is the rare and interesting one: net cash raised as debt that the balance sheet does not show as debt, which is the pattern of a grant booked as a loan. Before a gap is reported, the readings a filer plausibly meant are tried: short-term bank debt counted as borrowing, an untagged financing remainder as an untagged repayment, and all of financing less what went to and from the owners. adjustment names the reading that closed it.

Where a gap here is matched, within the same room and in the other direction, by an untagged remainder or a contrary line outside financing, offset_by names it. A reclassification moves an amount from one activity to another and leaves the total unchanged, so it shows up as two equal and opposite gaps.

How often it fires

Of 4,304 Danish filings for 2020-2024, 328 tag a cash flow statement. The class B companies that make up most of the corpus may leave it out. Across those 328:

  • the activities sum to the change in cash in 320 of 336 statements, and the roll-forward closes in 313 of 325, 35 of them only with the exchange rate adjustment;

  • "borrowed more than owed" is reported for 10 of the 196 filings with debt to check. That is a lead and not a finding: a loan drawn and repaid within the year, or debt classified differently in the two statements, can look the same from the outside;

  • a gap matched by an equal and opposite line elsewhere is found once, in the harmless direction: debt that grew 1.3 million more than was borrowed, beside an untagged 1.3 million in investing, which looks like an asset bought on credit. "borrowed more than owed" with its other half named, the signature of a grant booked as a loan, is found in none. Greenland Airports' 2025 group accounts, read separately, show it to the krone.

Planted in the 61 clean statements that tag their borrowing, a grant booked as a loan is flagged in 34 at 5% of the borrowing, 48 at 10% and 54 at 35%, while the internal checks still pass in 60 of the 61. At 5% the planted gap is the size of the room itself, so many fall inside it: rel is the price of not flagging every lease.

The signs are the filer's, read through the taxonomy

Filers write an outflow either as a negative figure or as a positive one under an outflow element, and both conventions are common. The taxonomy's balance attribute says which element is which: debit is an inflow, credit an outflow. Which convention a filing uses is read from its own gross outflows. If most of them are positive, an outflow element is subtracted as it stands. Otherwise every figure is taken as reported.

Neither reading uses abs(). A filer who tags an increase in capital as a negative CashCapitalReduction meant an inflow, and the arithmetic should treat it that way. The sign check is what reports the tag.

See also

check_statement() and check_cascade() for the other two statements, check_continuity() for figures stated in two filings.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
cf <- check_cashflow(x)

# the internal arithmetic
table(cf$check, cf$verdict)

# cash raised as debt that the balance sheet does not show as debt
cf[cf$verdict == "borrowed more than owed", ]
} # }
